en: Preface to the Essential Heart-Mantra of Cundī:
The virtues of all Bodhisattvas are inconceivable; how much more so for her who is called the Mother of the Seven Koṭis of Buddhas!
The power of all dhāraṇīs is immeasurable; how much more so for her who is called the Queen of Dhāraṇīs! Therefore, one should recite the mantra of Cundī.
The King swiftly extinguishes the four grave offenses and the five heinous crimes. For those who uphold this divine mantra, samādhi and wisdom arise instantaneously;

evil is extinguished and goodness is produced. How supreme is its efficacy! My teacher, the Venerable Master Changshou Xiang, has for many years faithfully practiced and recited the divine mantra of Cundī.
One day, he showed me a volume titled *The Essential Core of the Cundī Dhāraṇī* and said to me:
"This is the Dharma. Its practice is simple and easy; its efficacy is divine and swift. It will be of great benefit to those who practice it in this degenerate age.
I request that you, sir, add further national instruction to it and have it carved for publication in the world.
If so, how could its benefits be few? Hearing these words, I joyfully consented. I subsequently performed the collation and transmission to the carver, and wrote several verses as a preface.
The title is inscribed at the head of this volume.
On the day of the *pravāraṇā* ceremony for the monastic community in the seventh month of the year of Gichi (1709),
by the śramaṇa Huitan of Fangu Valley on Mount Tiantai, respectfully composed as a preface.
Preface to the *Cundī-hṛdaya-sāra*:
The scripture states that in the Buddha-lands there are no women. Those who interpret this say: "Those women who attain Buddhahood all transform into [men]."
Regarding the marks of a Buddha, she no longer possesses the conventional characteristics of a woman. Why, then, is Queen Cundī alone designated by the title "Mother of Buddhas"?
One day, while prostrating before her, a thought suddenly arose: "The word 'mother' (mātr) signifies the meaning of nurturing and raising;
it is a term for compassionate love. Indeed, the supervision and reprimands of a father or teacher cannot be applied at the very beginning of one's life, whereas the mother..."
Their diligent toil is uniquely able to suit the nature of their infant children. The precepts of the ancient Buddhas are exceedingly strict;
this is the way of paternal teachers in their instruction. The guidance of Cundī is exceedingly broad; this is the virtue of a compassionate mother. Why is this?
Because the ancient Buddhas desire for sentient beings to transcend the world, they must strictly establish defenses and admonish them directly, saying: "O person..."
One who is attached to beautiful forms cannot attain Buddhahood; you need not necessarily have a wife or children.
One who is cruel by nature cannot attain Buddhahood; you need not necessarily eat the flesh of sentient beings.
One whose nature is deluded and distracted cannot attain Buddhahood; you need not necessarily let your fingers touch or your lips sip fine wine and delicious spirits.
That teaching may be called rigorous. Consequently, among sentient beings, those capable would follow it, while those incapable would depart from it.
King Cūḍāmaṇi feared that those who would follow it would be few, while those who would depart would be many; therefore, he established a law to entice them, saying:
"If you can follow my teaching, I permit you to have wives and children; it is sufficient simply that you do not engage in sexual misconduct. You...
"If you can follow my instructions, I will permit you to eat meat to satisfy your hunger; it is sufficient that you observe the fasts and precepts once a month.
If you can follow my instructions, I will permit you to take fine wine and taste it sparingly;
it is sufficient that you remain self-restrained and do not become intoxicated. If you do not trust me, I shall grant you whatever you seek as an official."

"Ranks [of nobility], like kinsmen, like precious jewels, and like elixirs of immortality that are difficult to obtain—all these can greatly satisfy your hearts simply by following my teaching and reciting my mantra.
You shall not be rejected from entering my teaching on account of drinking wine, eating meat, or having a wife and children.
Do you see how broad and accessible my teaching is? Thereupon, the assembly...
Those sentient beings who follow the Buddha hear the name of Cundī and believe in and turn toward her;
even those sentient beings who do not follow the Buddha hear the name of Cundī and likewise believe in and turn toward her. Why is this so?
Human nature fears the severity of a father or teacher, yet delights in the leniency of a mother.

Thus, those who practice the Dharma of the World-Honored One fear its difficulty, whereas those who practice the Dharma of Cundī delight in its leniency; is this not the origin of the name "Buddha-Mother"?

Nevertheless, while the founder of the teaching has already established it as lenient, those who uphold the teaching should desire to be strict, surely embodying the love of a compassionate mother for her child.
The mind must be as if standing on the brink of a deep abyss or treading upon thin ice. One must advance whenever there is good and recognize and reform whenever there is fault;
only then can one establish oneself and bring glory to one's name.

If you were to rely on your mother’s leniency and believe she would not hold you accountable, and thus indulge your passions until you fell into transgression, even a mother of saintly virtue could not provide a refuge for you. This is—
How tragic! This is indeed something to be feared. Those who serve Cundī must cultivate such contemplations;
only then will they accord with the intent of Cundī. Let these words serve as the preface.

On the day of the winter solstice in the year Renzi of the Heavenly Stems and Branches cycle, the Buddhist disciple Shi Yao Ting of Min composed this record of the precious image, having purified himself through ritual bathing and prostrations.

The precious image of the Buddha-Mother Cundī possesses immeasurable radiance. Her marks and signs are complete, and her body is yellowish-white in color. She sits with legs crossed in the full lotus posture.
Her upper garment and lower robe are both made of white gauze with floral patterns; her body is draped with necklaces and garlands, and a svastika mark appears upon her chest.

A sash is tied around her waist, and a morning-glow scarf is draped over her person. On her wrists she wears bracelets of white conch shells, and on her upper arms bracelets of the seven precious gems. Both...
Her ears are adorned with precious pendants; her fingers are marked by rings. Upon her head she wears a flower crown, from which the five Tathāgatas manifest.
Her face has three eyes, the color of which is clear and limpid; they gaze downward upon sentient beings, giving rise to a mind of compassion. Her entire body possesses eighteen arms;
the two upper hands form the gesture of preaching the Dharma (or alternatively, the Cintāmaṇi-cundā mudrā), while the second left hand holds a wish-fulfilling jewel.
To the right of the banner, he bestows fearlessness. His third left hand holds a red lotus flower, and his third right hand holds a sword.
His fourth left hand holds a *kamaṇḍalu* (also rendered as a "washing vessel"), and his fourth right hand holds a *maṇi* rosary (also rendered as holding a "jeweled garland").

His fifth left hand holds a vajra-noose, and his fifth right hand holds a *ciñcāpūlaka* fruit (in Chinese, "fruit full of seeds"; it does not exist here [in China] but exists in the Western lands). His sixth hand...

The left hand holds a wheel and the right hand holds a battle-axe (*paraśu*). In the seventh pair of hands, the left holds a Dharma-conch (also known as *śaṅkha*) and the right holds a hook (*aṅkuśa*).
In the eighth pair of hands, the left holds a vase of excellence (also known as a *cintāmaṇi* vase) and the right holds a *vajra* (also known as a *vajra-ghaṇṭā*).
In the ninth pair of hands, the left holds the *Prajñāpāramitā* Sūtra and the right holds a jewel garland (alternatively, it is said to hold a rosary). He sits upon a lotus flower. The flower...
Below, there are two dragon kings providing protection; this is a general outline of the precious image.

If a practitioner who maintains the recitation wishes to visualize the precious image, they should perform this contemplation. If one is unable to perform such contemplation, one may proceed according to what is convenient.

One should carefully contemplate a single object (the object held in one of the eighteen hands)—then thoughts will become sincere and unified, and no further delusions will arise. This is called the "Secret of Mind."
Furthermore, the recitation of mantras constitutes the secret of speech, and the binding of mudrās constitutes the secret of body; this is called the correspondence of the three secrets.

Only those of superior faculties who maintain the recitation can achieve this. If practiced for a long time without interruption, one will obtain vast merit and shall attain progress toward Bodhi in this very life.
Recorded on the ninth day of the ninth month in the Gui-chou year.
The ritual implements within the eighteen-armed Treasure Image (Bǎoxiàng) currently transmitted in this world differ between various traditions.
Yáo Tǐng has meticulously examined the extant texts of the sutras and liturgical manuals, weighing them against the most appropriate standards.

He has recorded these findings in writing so that those who practice visualization in the future may have a basis for their practice, and those who create images may likewise have a standard to follow.
The method for the *saṃciti-mudrā*, the Great Samaya Seal:
With both hands palms upturned and extended, press the right hand over the left; the two thumbs should have their fingernails touching one another.
Place it below the navel center. After stabilizing body and mind, release the seal at the crown of the head.
This seal can extinguish all wild, distracted discursive thoughts and defiled mental activity.

For the Vajra Fist Mudrā, the thumbs press against the first joints of the ring fingers. While pressing, recite the syllable *Oṃ*. The remaining four fingers grasp the thumbs one by one to form the fist.
Recite the four *Hūṃ* syllables sequentially; when the mantra recitation is finished, likewise recite the five *Hūṃ* syllables sequentially.
Successively open the five fingers to form the Dispelling Seal. ○ This seal can eliminate internal and external obstacles and defilements, and accomplish all meritorious virtues.
It is the Cundī Seal.

Interlace the ring fingers and little fingers of both hands within; the right fingers press down upon the left (the left fingers are layered near the chest and the right fingers are layered on the outside).
Hold the two middle fingers upright and pressed against each other. Bend the two index fingers to rest against the first joint (one tradition says the side of the second joint) of the middle fingers.
Place the two thumbs side by side, pinching the middle joint of the right ring finger. While thus folding the fingers, recite nine times.
This is the Holy Brahma-Syllable Seal (*ārya-brahmākṣara-mudrā*). When one wishes to summon [the deity], move the two index fingers back and forth.
Upon finishing the recitation of the mantra, raise the seal to the crown of the head and open both hands. Using the *khaḍga* (sword) mudrā for each hand, recite the syllable *HŪṂ* and release them.

By this seal, the Bodhisattva will immediately come to provide protection; it can eliminate all karmic obstacles, and the accumulation of immeasurable merit and virtue will all be manifested before one.
To swiftly realize unsurpassed bodhi:
for the *xiangsheng* (resonant sound) mudrā, press the tip of the middle finger with the thumb; bend the finger to rest against the first joint of the middle finger. Strike once.
Mentally recite the single syllable *HŪṂ*.

All the mudrās mentioned above primarily constitute the secret of the body (*kāyaguhyaka*). If one does not understand these various mudrās, merely forming the vajra-fist (*vajramuṣṭi*) also constitutes the secret of the body.
Furthermore, there is the method of "scattered maintenance" (*saṃkṣiptadhāraṇa*); this may be maintained during any activity—walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—and one need only maintain it.
Oṃ jvale. For the mantra below, there is no need to form mudrās, no need to count recitations, no need for visualization, and no need to face a Buddha or a mirror;
simply reciting it orally suffices. When practiced authentically, it can eliminate afflictions and bring about the blissful Dharmakāya.
The Outer Form of the Cundī Seal,
the Inner Form of the Cundī Seal,
and the Vajra Fist.
Regarding the ritual procedure for holding and reciting the Great Samādhi Seal (Mahāsamādhi-mudrā),
the mantra-practitioner must establish a mirror altar. One should take a new mirror that has never been used before, with the face of the mirror facing west.
The practitioner faces east. On the fifteenth day of each month, at night, they should provide offerings according to their means.
Forming the Cundī mudrā at the heart, they should recite the mantra over a mirror one hundred and eight times. Thereafter, they should maintain the regular recitation of the mantra as usual.
Having finished bowing before a mirror while burning incense every morning and evening, one should then visualize the images of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas,
each manifesting immeasurable radiance and marks of excellence (lakṣaṇa-vyañjana), and maintain mindfulness of them as they appear before one.
Namo to the Seven Koṭi Buddhas’ Mother, the Great Holy Cundīrājñī Bodhisattva (three prostrations or one).
Namo to all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the Cundī Assembly (one prostration).

Homage to all the holy assemblies who protect the Dharma and guard the mantras at the Cundī assembly (one prostration). Having finished the prostrations, recite the Universal Offering Mantra as follows:
Oṃ oṃ oṃ sarvadharmā-vajra hūṃ. (Recite this mantra of universal offering within the mouth. In the hands, one must form the general auspicious mudrā. As for the method of this mudrā:

with the right hand, join the thumb and the ring finger together, while the remaining three fingers are all extended outward. With this very mudrā, seal all ritual vessels. Naturally, throughout the entire Dharma-realm, there will be inexhaustible offerings of incense, flowers, lamps, unguents, banners, pennants, and delicacies to perform worship.

This serves as an expression of devotion. If one lacks various items such as incense and flowers, or other implements for making offerings, merely reciting this mantra and forming this mudrā will likewise accomplish inexhaustible offerings.)

[Arrange] the ritual implements. Once the recitation of the mantra is finished, perform the *mudrā* of scattering [the flowers] upon the crown of the head. Kneeling, offer this prayer: "I, the disciple [Name], uphold this divine mantra.
I pray for [state the specific request]. May it be fulfilled as desired. Then, prostrate once and rise. (Note:

According to the *Xianmi yuantong*, whenever one makes a request, one must first recite the Cundī-bodhisattva-dhāraṇī five hundred thousand times, or seven hundred thousand times, or one million times as a preliminary practice. Only after that should one recite the mantra; then the request will certainly be accomplished. If one seeks supramundane dharmas, one should beforehand recite the Cundī-bodhisattva-dhāraṇī five...)

Recite one million times, or seven million times, or ten million times as a preliminary practice; thereafter, recite the mantra (it will certainly produce miraculous efficacy). Then, sit in the Vajra posture (pressing the right foot upon the left thigh;
alternatively, one may sit according to one's preference), and form the Great Samādhi Mudrā with the hands. Visualize that upon the crown of your head there is the Sanskrit syllable *Lam*.
This syllable is permeated by radiance like a bright jewel or the full moon. Thereafter, recite [the mantra].

Mantra. (For those who cannot visualize the Sanskrit characters, simply reciting the mantra with single-minded devotion is sufficient to possess all samādhis; other cases are to be understood accordingly).

Alternatively, one may further visualize the characters transforming into a wheel of fire that completely incinerates one’s own body of outflows (*āsrava*). Then, visualize that upon a great lotus flower, the letter *A* arises, forming the body of non-outflow wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna-kāya*).
Next, visualize the letter *Am* performing the empowerment (*abhiṣeka*). Finally, visualize the letter *Lam*.
The syllable transforms into a great fire that burns this conditioned world, just as the fire at the end of an eon consumes everything until nothing remains, leaving only empty stillness.
Then, one should visualize the establishment of the unconditioned altar.
At the very bottom, one should visualize the syllable *khaṃ* in various colors as the wheel of space (*ākāśa-cakra*). Above the wheel of space, one should visualize the syllable *haṃ* in black.
It transforms into a wind mandala (*vāyu-maṇḍala*). Upon the wind mandala, one should visualize everywhere the syllable *laṃ*, red in color, which transforms into a fire mandala (*tejo-maṇḍala*).
Upon the fire mandala, one should visualize everywhere the syllable *vaṃ*, white in color, which transforms into a water mandala (*ap-maṇḍala*).

Upon the water mandala, one should visualize everywhere the syllable *aṃ*, yellow in color, which transforms into a vajra-ground (*vajra-bhūmi*). Upon the vajra-ground, one should visualize everywhere...
There is a great lotus flower. Upon each and every lotus flower is the Bodhisattva Cundī, surrounded by immeasurable assemblies of holy beings.
Before each and every Cundī is the practitioner’s own self.
From each and every self emerge immeasurable flowers, fruits, food, drink, banners, pennants, and other various articles of offering, which are used to make offerings. Furthermore, they all...

Regarding the Three Mysteries Correspondence for the Cundī Mirror Altar: (Furthermore, if the practitioner lacks an image of Cundī and offerings such as flowers, fruits, food, and drink, merely performing this visualization will also bring about auspicious accomplishment.

For those unable to visualize the fire-wheel, the empowerment, or the establishment of the unconditioned altar and so forth, they may simply rely on the method described above, visualizing the syllable upon the crown of the head like a bright jewel or a full moon;
this alone is sufficient. Having completed the visualization, hold pure water and recite the Cundī Dhāraṇī twenty-one times toward the zenith, nadir, and the eight directions.

Sprinkling [water] upon it immediately establishes the boundary for warding off obstacles (for those who do not wish to sprinkle water, they may gesture with their hands as if sprinkling water while visualizing the act; this is equivalent to actual sprinkling).

Next, recite the Mantra of Purifying the Dharmadhātu twenty-one times. With the left hand forming the vajra-fist and the right hand holding the rosary (either kneeling or sitting as convenient), recite the mantra as follows:
Oṃ-lam (visualize the Sanskrit syllable).
Next, recite the protection mantra twenty-one times. The mantra is:
Oṃ-kṣiṃ (the syllable *kṣiṃ* is pronounced with a retroflex *ṛ*-like sound and a falling tone; visualize the Sanskrit syllable).
Next, recite the six-syllable Great Illumination Mantra one hundred and eight times.

The mantra is: Oṃ maṇi padme hūṃ. (Visualize the Sanskrit syllables radiating light. Furthermore, imagine yourself as perfectly complete, pure white, and pervaded by light. Contemplate within your mind:
"May the bodies of all sentient beings attain complete purity and remain unstained by afflictions.")
Having finished the recitation, place the vajra-fist seal upon the forehead. Next, seal the left shoulder and the right shoulder.

Next, seal the heart, the throat, and the crown of the head, dispersing [the mudrā] from the crown. While sealing these five places, recite the five *hūṃ* syllables in succession; when dispersing, recite them in succession as well.
Spread the five fingers and recite the syllable *HŪṂ* five times in succession.
Next, recite the Cundī Dhāraṇī while forming the Cundī Mudrā with both hands.

Recite the Cundī Dhāraṇī and the One-Syllable Mahācakra Dhāraṇī together one hundred and eight times. (If one is unable to form the Cundī Mudrā, follow the previous method by forming it with the left hand.)

The Vajra Fist: Hold a rosary in the right hand. When forming the Cundī mudrā and wishing to count the recitations, count upon one's own fingers or upon the arm of the Bodhisattva Cundī. If one is in a hurry, simply hold it loosely.

Alternatively, for those who do not prefer the Mahācakra mantra, it is also permissible to hold only the Cundī Dhāraṇī. Or, for those unable to recite according to the sequence of mantras such as the "Universal Offering to the Pure Dharma Realm," it is also permissible to hold only the Cundī Dhāraṇī.
Furthermore, for those of dull faculties, it is sufficient to hold only from the syllable *Oṃ* onwards.
I prostrate and take refuge in Susiddhi; with head bowed to the ground, I pay homage to the seventy million [deities]. I now praise the Great Cundī;
I pray that you will look upon me with compassion and grant your protection. (Recite once.)
The mantra of the Heart of the Great Cundī Dhāraṇī of the Seven Koṭis of Buddhas is as follows:
Namaḥ samantabuddhakoṭīnām | tadyathā | oṃ cale cule cuḷe cunde svāhā | oṃ pūle ||
[Recite] (2-syllable) [2-syllable] (2-syllable).
Having finished the recitation, perform the *Cundī* mudrā by scattering [flowers] over the crown of the head; or, having bound the mudrā, one may recite it one thousand and eighty times.

It is best to perform it all at once. Alternatively, one may recite one hundred and eight times; for the remainder, simply form the *vajra-mudrā* with the left hand while holding the prayer beads with the right hand.

One may maintain the practice for three hundred times, five hundred times, seven hundred times, one thousand and eighty times, three thousand, five thousand times, or even an incalculable number of times—reciting as many times as one’s capacity allows is acceptable.
However, for the one hundred and eight recitations, one should hold the mantra from the syllable *Oṃ* onwards (beginners should ideally hold the entire mantra;

those who do not wish to hold the full mantra may generally hold it from *Oṃ* onwards; those who do not wish to hold it from *Oṃ* onwards should hold the entire mantra from beginning to end). Furthermore, there are five types of maṇḍala rituals: the rites of pacification (*śāntika*), enrichment (*pauṣṭika*), magnetizing (*vaśya*), subjugation (*abhicāruka*), and supramundane (*lokottara*).

Each of these has its own distinctions; simply follow the aforementioned method when performing them. Whatever one seeks will certainly be accomplished. For details, see the *Xianmi yuantong* (Complete Penetration of Exoteric and Esoteric Teachings). ○ Furthermore, the correct...

When reciting, one must not engage in conversation with others before completing one hundred and eight recitations. If one wishes to speak, one should visualize a syllable upon the tongue; even if conversation occurs, it will not constitute an interruption.
Having finished the recitation, recite the Mantra for Completing and Amending Deficiencies ten times.
The mantra is: Oṃ hulu hulu svāhā.
Homage to the Great Holy Cundī Queen, Mother of Seven Koṭis of Buddhas (three prostrations or one).
Homage to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas in the assembly of Cundī (one prostration).
Homage to all the holy multitudes who protect the Dharma and guard the mantra in the assembly of Cundī (one prostration).
Having completed the prostrations, collect the mirror and place it in its pouch. The ritual for the recitation above is now complete.
The mantra for general offering is: *Oṃ āḥ oṃ namaḥ sarvabuddhabodhisattvebhyaḥ hūṃ*. Add the auspicious [concluding verses].

The seal of auspiciousness (*śrī-mudrā*) can cause inexhaustible incense, flowers, lamps, ointments, banners, flags, parasols, canopies, robes, bedding, pavilions, palaces, lion thrones, music, song, dance, and various kinds of exquisite delicacies to pervade the entire dharma-realm.
These fill the expanse of space as offerings to manifest one's sincere devotion. If one lacks such incense, flowers, and so forth—
Regarding various articles for making offerings: simply recite this mantra and form this mudrā, and they will likewise become inexhaustible offering articles (*ananta-pūjopakaraṇa*).

(This mantra originally does not belong to the Cundī [Dhāraṇī]. Ancient masters, fearing that those who recited the Cundī might lack the means for offerings when performing acts of reverence, supplemented this mantra at the beginning.)
Oṃ-lam. This is the mantra of the pure *dharmadhātu*. Visualize the single syllable *lam*, which is able to cause the three karmas to become entirely purified.
All sinful obstructions will be completely eliminated. Furthermore, it can accomplish all supreme matters.
Wherever one dwells, everything becomes pure. Even if clothing is impure, it becomes a pure garment. Even if the body has not been washed...
When bathing, if one uses water alone to perform purification, it is not called true purification. A single syllable of the mantra transforms defilement into purity. As the verse says:
"The syllable RA is brilliant white, adorned with the bindu of emptiness; like a bright jewel in a topknot, it is placed upon the crown of the head.
The mantra is identical to the Dharma-realm; immeasurable multitudes of sins are removed from all places of contact with impurity."
One should add this gateway of syllables. If external conditions are not fulfilled, one should simply purify with this syllable *laṃ*.
If external conditions are fulfilled, one first bathes with water, puts on new clean garments, and further purifies with the syllable.
This means that both the internal and external are completely purified.
*Oṃ kili* is the mantra for protecting the body. It can extinguish all sinful karma, including the five heinous crimes and the ten evil deeds;
it can eliminate all manner of suffering from illness, calamities, obstacles, evil dreams, malevolent spirits, ghosts, demons, and all other inauspicious occurrences. And...
It can accomplish all supreme matters and cause every aspiration to be fully realized. This mantra is the heart-essence of all Buddhas.
If a person recites it with single-minded devotion even once, they will be able to protect themselves;
no ghosts, spirits, celestial Māras, or demons will dare to approach them. Reciting it twice can protect one's companions. Reciting it three times can protect...
Reciting it four times can protect the people within a single household; reciting it up to seven times can protect the people of the four continents.
Oṃ maṇi padme hūṃ. This is the six-syllable Great Illumination Mantra.

If one recites this mantra, immeasurable Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings will assemble wherever one dwells. Furthermore, it possesses immeasurable samādhis and Dharma gates.
For the person who maintains and recites it, seven generations of their lineage shall all attain liberation. [The ailments] within the abdomen...
This insect shall attain the rank of a bodhisattva. This person will daily attain the perfect merit of the six pāramitās and obtain inexhaustible eloquence and a pure assembly of followers.

The breath emitted from their mouth, upon touching the bodies of others, shall cause those touched to be free from all poisonous anger; they shall attain the rank of a bodhisattva. Suppose, for instance, that four...
All people in the world shall attain the rank of a Bodhisattva of the seventh stage.
All the merits possessed by those Bodhisattvas are equal and no different from the merit of reciting this six-syllable mantra once.

This mantra is the subtle and wondrous fundamental mind of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva. If a person transcribes this Six-Syllable Great Illuminator (Ṣaḍakṣarī Mahāvidyā), it is equivalent to transcribing [the entire canon].
The merit obtained from the eighty-four thousand treasuries of the Dharma is equal and without distinction.

Even if one were to fashion images of the Tathāgata out of gold and jewels as numerous as motes of dust, it would not equal the merit of writing down even a single character from among these six characters.
If a person attains the recitation of this six-syllable Great Mantra (*ṣaḍakṣarī mahāvidyā*), they cannot be defiled by greed, hatred, or delusion.
If one wears this mantra upon their body, they likewise will not be defiled by the afflictions of greed, hatred, and delusion.
All sentient beings touched by the hands of such a wearer or beheld by their eyes will swiftly attain the rank of a Bodhisattva.
One shall never again undergo the sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, death, and so forth.
When these six syllables of the Great Illumination (Mahāvidyā) were fully proclaimed, seventy-seven koṭis of Buddhas appeared simultaneously and, with one voice, recited the Cundī Dhāraṇī.
Thus, it is known that this six-syllable Great Illumination and the Cundī Mantra are mutually dependent in their sequence.
Namo saptānāṃ samyaksaṃbuddhakoṭīnām | tadyathā | oṃ cale cule cuḍe svāhā | This Cundī Dhāraṇī is able to extinguish all karmic obstructions of the five heinous crimes and the ten evil deeds,
and brings to fulfillment all pure dharmas and meritorious virtues. For one who upholds this mantra, regardless of whether they are a layperson or a monastic...

Even if one lives at home, drinks alcohol, eats meat, and has a wife and children, without discriminating between the pure and the impure, merely by maintaining the practice with a sincere heart, one can cause short-lived sentient beings to increase their lifespan immeasurably. Even leprosy (*kāmalā*) can be cured, let alone other illnesses;
it is impossible for such diseases not to be extinguished. If one recites this for a full forty-nine days, [the power of] Cundī Bodhisattva...

Śākyamuni commanded two holy beings to constantly follow that person. Whatever good or evil they do, and whatever thoughts arise in their minds, both shall be reported to them one by one at their ears.

If there are those who lack merit or auspicious marks, who fail to attain office despite seeking it, or who are oppressed by poverty and suffering, if they constantly recite this mantra, they will be able to obtain in the present life the blessings of a Wheel-Turning King, and the official rank they seek will certainly be attained.
One’s wishes shall be fulfilled. If one seeks wisdom, one shall obtain great wisdom; if one seeks sons or daughters, one shall obtain sons and daughters.
Whatever one seeks, there is nothing that will not be fulfilled, just as a wish-fulfilling jewel (cintāmaṇi) accords with every desire.
Furthermore, by reciting this mantra, one can cause kings, ministers, and the four classes of beings to feel love and respect; upon seeing them, they shall immediately rejoice.
One who recites this mantra cannot be drowned by water, nor burned by fire.
Poisons, enemies, military arrays, powerful thieves, as well as fierce dragons, wild beasts, and various malevolent spirits, shall all be unable to cause harm.

If one wishes to invite Brahmā, Śakra, the Four Heavenly Kings, or Yama, the Son of Heaven, it suffices merely to recite this mantra; they will surely arrive according to the invitation. Not... [omitted].
I venture to come forward next. All that is required for its employment shall be obtained according to one's will. This mantra possesses great power within Jambudvīpa;
it can move Mount Sumeru and dry up the waters of the great ocean. It can cause flowers and fruits to grow even upon withered, parched wood.
How much more so if one can further recite the mantra according to the ritual; without changing one's physical body, one will attain great supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) and go to Tuṣita Heaven.

If one seeks longevity or various elixirs of the immortals, simply by reciting the mantra according to the ritual, one will immediately behold Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva or Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva, who will bestow upon one the wondrous medicine of the immortals. One may take it as desired and consume it.
One will immediately attain the path of the immortals, obtain an extended lifespan equal to that of the sun and moon, and realize the stage of a Bodhisattva.

If one recites [the mantra] according to the ritual one million times, one shall be able to travel to the pure lands of the ten directions, attend upon all Buddhas, universally hear the wondrous Dharma, and realize Bodhi.
Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna praised it with a verse concerning the merit of Cundī: The Merit of Cundī: [Verse follows]
If one constantly recites this [mantra] with a concentrated and tranquil mind, no great calamities whatsoever shall be able to harm such a person.
Whether in the heavens or among humans, they shall receive blessings equal to those of a Buddha. Having encountered this wish-fulfilling jewel, one will certainly attain that which is peerless.
Oṃ bhrūṃ. This is the single-syllable Great Wheel mantra; it is also known as the Single-Syllable Heart Mantra of the Final Dharma Age.

During the time of the Final Dharma, when the Dharma is about to perish, this mantra possesses great power to bring about vast benefit for the world, to protect all the Dharma-treasuries of the Tathāgata, and to subjugate all the eight classes of supernatural beings. It can...
It destroys all evil spells in the world; it is the crown of all Buddhas and the heart-essence of Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva.
It can bestow fearlessness upon all sentient beings and grant happiness to all sentient beings.
For those who practice and uphold it, they shall obtain results according to their wishes. Like a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*), it can fulfill all aspirations. If one recites this...
Recite this mantra. Within a radius of five hundred *yojanas* in the four directions, all malevolent spirits and ghosts will scatter in flight of their own accord;
no malevolent planets or celestial demons (*deva-māra*) shall dare to approach.
If one fears that other mantras will not achieve success when recited, one should recite this mantra together with those other mantras in the same session, and they will certainly be accomplished.
If [the practitioner] does not achieve success or manifest signs of efficacy, the deity of the mantra and others shall have their heads split into seven pieces.
Know that this mantra can assist all other mantras in attaining swift accomplishment; alternatively, one may also hold this mantra separately.
Oṃ hulu hulu jaya mukhe svāhā. This is the mantra for fulfilling deficiencies.
It is used to compensate for the omissions in various mantras so that their complete efficacy may be attained.

For anyone who maintains these mantras, should there be a lack of hand gestures (*mudrā*), improper sequential visualization, a lack of focused concentration, or interruptions in recitation and retention— [The above mantra is applied to rectify such faults.]
Even if one recites this mantra for but a single thought-moment, there will be merit and no transgression;
therefore, it is appended hereafter as an aid to the Cundī Dhāraṇī (this mantra was originally not part of the Cundī cycle, having been incorporated from another source, hence the term "appended").
If one can recite the mantra according to the Dharma, then all benevolent deities, dragon kings, and Vajrapāṇi will constantly follow and protect them,
never leaving their side, guarding them as they would their own eyes or their own life.

If there are sentient beings who, even with a distracted mind, recite this divine mantra with their mouths, they will always be followed and guarded day and night by immeasurable members of the retinue of the Vajragarbha-rāja Bodhisattvas.
Even if the Māra-king should seek an opportunity against them, he will ultimately find none. Lesser spirits and ghosts shall remain ten *yojanas* away from these virtuous people.
If the retinues of Māra should come to harass these virtuous persons, the hosts of Vajras shall shatter their heads with precious vajras until they are like fine dust.
They shall always cause the deeds of these persons to be fulfilled according to their wishes.

(Even for one whose mind is not yet awakened and who possesses inherent distraction—such that they recite the mantra while distracted—they still possess such efficacy; how much more so for one who is undistracted?)

If the deceased has extensively committed evil karma and dies to fall into the three miserable realms, the practitioner of the *mantra* path shall recite the name of the deceased and single-mindedly chant the mantra.
The deceased will, at that moment, be able to leave the evil destinies and be reborn in the heavens.

(If the deceased has not committed evil karma, there is no doubt they will be reborn in heaven through the power of the mantra. All persons of benevolence, filial piety, and compassion should pay particular heed to this.)
Attaining Buddhahood by means of other gates is like traveling a thousand *li* by riding a sheep or a horse; it takes a long time before one arrives.
Attaining Buddhahood by means of the *dhāraṇī* gate is like traveling a thousand *li* by riding a divine vehicle; one arrives as soon as the thought arises.
Although the destination reached is no different, there is a difference in speed between the vehicles upon which one rides.
For those who maintain and recite this mantra, all that they seek shall be fulfilled; however, this excludes those who harbor doubts toward the mantra (those who do not have deep faith).
For such as these, the recitation of the mantra will certainly yield no efficacy. Do not be surprised if the mantra appears to be without merit.
The above explains the efficacy of the mantra.
When reciting it daily, one must fix upon a specific time. If recited once, it should be fixed for the morning; if recited twice—
Add the evening. Maintain the practice during samādhi. Add midday. For those with busy affairs, there is no restriction on the time;

if one has leisure, maintain the practice. (If one has business during the day, maintain it at night. If one is too preoccupied to manage it, then in all dealings with people and affairs, maintain it in a "scattered" manner. [Note:
"Scattered maintenance" means not forming mudrās, not counting recitations, not facing a mirror, and not performing visualizations. )
There are five types of recitation according to one's faculties and preferences. First is the yoga-recitation:
visualize one’s own mind as a single moon disc, serene and pure, with its interior and exterior clearly distinct.
Arrange the nine sacred Brahma-syllables within this lunar disc, with the syllable *Oṃ* at the center, followed by *Jvale*, *Ujvale*, *Cundhe*, and *Svāhā*.

The syllable *HA* revolves from the front to the right, sequentially arrayed along the rim of the wheel, ending and beginning again. Second is the retention of the inhalation and exhalation (*ānāpāna-dhāraṇī*):
within the inhalation and exhalation, one visualizes the nine holy Brahma-syllables; as the breath goes out, the syllables go out, and as the breath comes in, the syllables come in.
Each syllable is vividly clear, like a string of bright pearls that must not be interrupted. Third is the Vajra-retention (*vajra-dhāraṇī*).
Without moving the lips or teeth, and without the tongue reaching the palate, one should move the mouth slightly and maintain four subtle sounds, audible only to one's own ears;
these should be neither too slow nor too hurried, with each syllable clearly articulated. Fifth is maintaining it at a loud voice so that others may hear it;
this also serves to extinguish transgressions.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of recitation: first, recitation without counting, which means not using a rosary, maintaining constant continuity without interruption;
second, recitation with counting, which means using a rosary and must limit the number each day, ensuring that none is omitted.

(If there are important matters that cause obstruction and the count is deficient, one must necessarily make up for it once the matter is concluded. Alternatively, if the limited number is small—no more than three or five hundred, or perhaps one or two hundred—it is permissible to exceed that number each day rather than falling short.)

Those of superior faculties must maintain the three secrets in correspondence: first, the secret of body, which is the binding of mudrās; second, the secret of speech, which is the recitation of mantras;

and third, the secret of mind, which consists of either visualizing the Sanskrit syllables of the mantra, or attending to the sound of the recitation, or visualizing the Bodhisattva Cundī, or visualizing the objects held in the Bodhisattva’s hands, such as the vajra, the flask, flowers, fruits, and so forth. If one employs these three secrets...
This serves as the gateway. It is not necessary to pass through kalpas of time to fully cultivate all practices; rather, one may fulfill all the pāramitās within this very life.

The practitioner need not undergo arduous discipline or exhaust the body, for fear that the mind and spirit will become distracted during the four postures of walking, standing, sitting, and lying down.
Within these rituals, one may practice the three secrets in all their aspects. Regarding seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, one should contemplate only the letter *A*.
The essential point is to diligently exert body and mind so as not to succumb to indolence. When one is about to attain accomplishment, various obstacles will inevitably arise;
one should then perform rites such as those for pacifying or subjugating, according to the specific differences in the practitioner’s nature and faculties. Within these...

In the interim, one will certainly attain the manifestation of samādhi; therein, within meditative concentration, one will behold countless Buddha assemblies, hear the sounds of the wondrous Dharma, and realize the rank of a Bodhisattva of the Ten Stages.
If, while one is reciting with intense urgency, various demonic obstacles should arise; or if one suddenly feels fear; or if the tongue finds it difficult to recite;
or if body and mind are restless; or if there is excessive anger or drowsiness; or if one perceives various strange signs;
or if one develops doubts toward the mantra and becomes unwilling to recite it (and so forth)—if one wishes to apply an antidote, one should contemplate as follows:
One should visualize the letter *ra* from the Sanskrit script, or visualize the letter *laṃ*, or visualize the letter *a*, and so forth.
By visualizing any one of these letters, that objective realm will naturally dissolve. If discursive thought is excessive, one should visualize the letter *sa*.

This immediately constitutes non-conceptualization. If there is an abundance of attachment to the mind of existence, one should contemplate the character "Han" (含), which signifies that the dharmas of causes and conditions are fundamentally empty.
The above has been explained according to one particular approach. To speak of it in reality, however, any single character may be employed in all instances;
for a single character truly contains all characters and all functional capacities.
These are all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
When practitioners of the *mantra* path apply themselves with diligence in recitation, they may dream of various Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, holy monks, or celestial maidens;
or they may dream of themselves soaring through the air with ease, crossing the great ocean, floating upon rivers, or ascending towers.
They may see high mounds or trees; or they may ascend a white mountain; or they may ride upon lions, white horses, or white elephants;
or they may dream of beautiful flowers and fruits; or they may dream of śramaṇas wearing yellow or white robes; or they may eat white things and vomit black things.
Or swallowing the sun, moon, and so forth—these are signs of the extinction of beginningless sins. Or while reciting the mantra, one may see various rays of light;
or see extraordinary flowers covering the ground in the sky; or see Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, noble Saṃghas, celestial immortals, and the like;
or see the pure lands of the Buddhas; or travel personally to a Buddha-field to receive [the teachings] directly.
One makes offerings. Or one sees the light of lamps rise to a height of one or two chi, or even up to ten chi; or there is no fire, yet smoke naturally rises from within the incense burner.
Or one sees images of Buddhas, banners, and canopies move of their own accord. Or one hears the various beautiful voices of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Or one perceives one’s own body as majestic, lofty, and tall. Or teeth that have fallen out grow back again. Or the hair turns white.
Or one’s complexion turns black. Or the body becomes moist and white, such that fleas and lice do not arise. Or the afflictions of greed, hatred, and delusion naturally vanish.
Or one possesses *dhāraṇī*, never forgetting a single word while being able to expound upon manifold meanings.
Or wisdom suddenly arises, such that one naturally understands all sūtras, vinayas, and śāstras. Or all samādhi dharma-gates spontaneously manifest before one. Or merit...
"Virtue will suddenly soar, and the fourfold assembly will look up to you with devotion," and so forth.

If you encounter such circumstances as these, recognize them merely as signs of the increase of merit and wisdom and the proximity of accomplishment; do not give rise to a mind of doubt, nor entertain thoughts of acceptance or rejection.
One should contemplate that all encountered objects are the letter *A*, or the letter *Lam*, and so forth;
or one should imagine them all to be like dreams and illusions, or imagine them all to be the single mind of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

If such signs of efficacy are encountered, one must further rouse the three karmas and apply diligent effort to the recitation. One must not proclaim the experiences within the mantra, nor trade upon them for gain.
Regarding others: one may only speak of this to those who follow the same path, provided they do not seek fame or profit, and who offer respectful praise.
○ All that has been described above—such as seeing various rays of light and other phenomena while correctly reciting the mantra—is the actual text of the scripture.

Nowadays, there are idle monks and Confucian scholars who casually investigate the principles of Chan meditation; when they encounter these signs, they mistake them for strange portents or demonic anomalies. This is not so.
This is merely to slander the teachings of the Supreme Vehicle; it is also a false view that abandons appearances to grasp at intrinsic nature.
It is simply because one does not know that these appearances are originally of the nature of self-nature.
The above has explained the practice of mantra recitation.
Mantras are the secret teachings of the Tathāgata; they are understood by Buddhas alone without the need for verbal explanation.
Even Bodhisattvas on the causal stages cannot fathom their subtle purport, let alone ordinary worldlings who emerge from the mundane realm—how could they possibly grasp and expound them?
Nevertheless, although mantras are ineffable, the efficacy of the mantras and the practice of upholding them [are manifest].

The cultivation of these practices can indeed be described. If one is able to attain the functional efficacy through such practice and perseveres without ceasing, one will likewise transcend the stage of a bodhisattva on the causal level and ascend above it;
thus, that which was previously ineffable shall all become expressible. Written respectfully by the Buddha’s disciple Shi (Yao Ting).
Wherever this mantra resides, it will surely be protected by the eight classes of devas and nāgas, and its spiritual efficacy will be supreme.
Even those who are unable to recite it should worship it with a devout heart, enshrining it in the same place as the offerings to the Buddha and the household deities;
thus one shall obtain immeasurable merit. One must by no means place it in a confused or profane manner, lest one bring upon oneself the retribution for such irreverence.
Faults and errors are hereby acknowledged. Reverence! Reverence!
This is the woodblock edition preserved in the Cundī Hall at Houzhou, Fuxing Nantai.
